archetype.name: Pocket Passer (play-action rhythm vet)
archetype.definition: A 38-year-old, statue-still timing thrower who wins from a clean pocket with anticipation and the intermediate-to-deep game, gives almost nothing with his legs, and is unusually good at not taking sacks.

report.headline: The 2025 decline looks like a blip: vintage Cousins efficiency, inflated TD rate
report.take:
Cousins came into 2026 looking finished. His 2025 in Atlanta was the worst full stretch of his prime: 6.4 yards per attempt, a -2.8 CPOE and 0.024 EPA per play, ranked 35th. Eight games into his Raiders run he has swung all the way back to his Minnesota baseline. His 0.187 EPA per dropback ranks 14th and sits well above the league's 0.034. His yards per attempt is up 1.11 on last year and his CPOE has climbed back into positive territory. That is the same band he lived in from 2019 to 2021, so this reads as a return to form, not a career year out of nowhere.

What drives it is a more aggressive version of a familiar player. His 20.85% aggressiveness rate is the highest of his career, and the payoff is in the downfield buckets. On 28 deep attempts he has posted 0.785 EPA per attempt with a +7.4 CPOE and no picks. Throws of 10-plus air yards have added 51.5 EPA, against 14.8 on everything shorter. Brock Bowers is the engine: 0.535 EPA per target and 33.1 total, by far the most of anyone on the roster. Tre Tucker gives him a second efficient outlet. The pocket has held up, partly through his own doing. He holds the ball 2.9 seconds yet his sack rate ranks 5th and his pressure-to-sack rate ranks 3rd. He gets it out under duress rather than eating it, which was never his calling card in Minnesota and is the biggest quiet improvement here.

The numbers hide two things. First, the touchdown total runs ahead of the play-by-play. He has 15 red-zone touchdowns and no picks there, yet only a 0.37 success rate inside the 20. Add 10 third-down scores and a 6.7% TD rate against a league norm of 4.6, and the scoring is outrunning the underlying efficiency. Second, his accuracy has wobbled lately. CPOE was -9.7 against Buffalo and -7.9 against the Rams, and his last five games sit almost two points below his season mark. His 0.201 EPA per dropback in that stretch shows the downfield shots are still paying, but the completion rate on the routine stuff is slipping. The 1-4 record over that stretch is mostly not on him. Las Vegas has a bottom-three run game and a 25th-ranked defense, so he keeps throwing 38 times a game from behind.

The outlook is stable volume with some regression. The Raiders will keep passing because they can't run and can't stop people, which locks in his yardage floor. Expect the touchdown rate to drift back toward something closer to two a game than 2.4. The four intermediate interceptions are the risk to monitor for a 38-year-old throwing more aggressively than ever.

strengths.title: Downfield efficiency is back
strengths.body: His intermediate and deep throws are carrying the offense: 0.785 EPA per deep attempt with a +7.4 CPOE, from the most aggressive version of him on record. Everything from 10 air yards out has added far more EPA than his entire short game. Deep samples are small, so 28 attempts will cool, but the career line says he has always been a capable downfield anticipation thrower when protected.

strengths.title: Avoiding sacks without moving
strengths.body: He rarely runs and his scrambles lose value, yet only a small share of pressures become sacks, ranking 3rd. His overall sack rate is less than half the league's. That is a decision-making skill: he throws it away or finds the hot read rather than taking the drive-killer. It has improved on his Minnesota years, when he sat mid-pack, so some regression is possible. Still, it is a choice, not luck.

strengths.title: A real rebound from 2025
strengths.body: Last year's slide looked like age catching up, but this year's yards per attempt and CPOE are both up sharply. His EPA per dropback is back to where he sat during his best Vikings seasons. A better target group, led by Bowers, explains much of it. That makes it more durable than a hot streak.

concerns.title: Touchdown rate running ahead of efficiency
concerns.body: Fifteen red-zone touchdowns on a 0.37 red-zone success rate is a lot of finishing on a modest hit rate. His TD percentage sits 2.1 points over the league average. Some of it is real, because Bowers is a red-zone matchup problem. Expect the scoring to come down even if the yards hold.

concerns.title: Intermediate picks and middle accuracy
concerns.body: Four of his five interceptions came on 10-19 yard throws. His CPOE over the middle of the field is -7.2. Recent games show the same wobble, with CPOE dipping in the last five weeks. That is the cost of his new aggressiveness: tighter windows over the middle at 38. It is a real flaw to watch rather than noise.

concerns.title: He has to carry everything
concerns.body: The run game ranks 30th in EPA and the defense 25th, which explains a 1-4 stretch despite good passing. That props up his volume, but it also means predictable dropbacks against defenses that know the run isn't coming. It is a team problem, not his. It will persist, and so will his heavy throwing load.

trend.note: His passing EPA has been positive in seven of eight games, with the Rams dud the lone exception, followed by his best game of the year at the Jets. Completion accuracy has bounced around more than the overall efficiency has.

nextGame.headline: Ten-point underdog in San Francisco means volume, but few chunk plays
nextGame.body:
San Francisco is the worst possible run matchup for an offense that already can't run. The 49ers rank 1st against the rush and 1st in explosive runs allowed, so this game goes through Cousins. With the Raiders getting 10 points and a 51.5 total behind the league's No. 2 offense, he should be throwing from behind all day. The catch is that this defense smothers exactly what has driven his season. It ranks 3rd in explosive pass rate allowed and 7th on deep throws, while giving up plenty underneath (24th on short passes). Expect a dink-and-dunk volume game rather than his usual chunk-play efficiency.

Availability on the 49ers side matters most. Nick Bosa "has a chance" to return from his knee injury. Without him, this pass rush ranks near the bottom in hit rate, which suits a quarterback who already avoids sacks. Safety Marques Sigle (88% of snaps) and slot corner Upton Stout are also questionable. Losing either would loosen the coverage over the middle, where Bowers works. On offense San Francisco may get back Christian McCaffrey, Mike Evans and Deebo Samuel after the bye. That raises the shootout odds and Cousins' passing volume. The Raiders have no injury that touches him.

keyMatchups.title: Run game versus the league's best
keyMatchups.body: Las Vegas ranks 30th in rushing EPA and San Francisco 1st in rush defense. Any early-down run is likely a wasted down, which pushes the whole game onto Cousins' arm. That boosts his attempts but lengthens third downs.

keyMatchups.title: Explosive-pass lid on his deep game
keyMatchups.body: His season runs on 10-plus-yard throws, and the 49ers rarely allow explosive completions. The soft spot is short passing, so this may be the week he wins with Bowers and backs on volume rather than shots.

keyMatchups.title: Shootout script from SF's offense
keyMatchups.body: San Francisco's offense ranks 2nd in EPA and 1st in success rate, with skill players potentially returning. Falling behind keeps Cousins throwing, as it did in his high-volume losses to Kansas City and Buffalo.

nextGame.watch: Whether Bosa plays: without him the pass rush is mild and Cousins can sit and work Bowers underneath; with him, a long-developing dropback offense gets tested.

restOfSeason.body:
The volume is the safest part of his profile. A broken run game and a leaky defense mean 35-plus attempts most weeks, and his sack avoidance keeps drives alive. I'd project 255-290 passing yards a game. The efficiency should stay above average, because the rebound is rooted in a better target group and a style he has played before. Some cooling on the deep ball is likely, though, since 28 attempts at that clip is not a rate anyone holds.

The touchdowns are where regression lands. The red-zone finishing and third-down scoring are outrunning his success rates, so 1.6-2.1 touchdowns a game is the realistic band rather than his current pace. Interceptions may tick up slightly, given the intermediate risk he is taking. Overall he looks like a reliable mid-teens to low-20s fantasy QB in an offense that will have to throw.
swingFactors: Whether intermediate picks pile up as he keeps pushing the ball

confidence.note: Eight solid starts and a strong career baseline, but the TD rate and deep-ball samples are small and he is 38.
